item.title: Research with Reach: Translating Evidence into Action for People and Work
item.content:encoded:
Tara S. Behrend, Michigan State University

Michael T. Braun, DePaul University

Nick Turner, University of Calgary

Chia-Huei Wu, King's College London

This special issue seeks empirical research demonstrating how evidence from industrial-organizational psychology translates into actionable improvements for individuals, organizations, and society. Submissions must provide clear pathways showing how findings inform decisions, policies, or interventions that stakeholders can implement, rather than simply identifying important workplace phenomena.

The issue prioritizes use-inspired research emerging from organizational challenges or practitioner collaborations, employing rigorous methods and articulating tangible impacts. Manuscripts should be contextualized within specific occupations or sectors, include applied deliverables such as implementation frameworks, and demonstrate broader societal contributions such as improvements in wellbeing, equity, or workforce development.

Submissions must articulate the problem addressed, research-based solution, and observed outcomes from implementation. Conceptual papers, reviews, and meta-analyses are unsuitable. Well-executed field-based work that meets the translational aims is welcome.

Appel publié par Personnel Psychology. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Culture and Behavior Change
  • Employee Well-Being and Societal Outcomes
  • Resilience and Recovery at Work
  • Psychological Recovery and Sustainable Performance
  • Work and Non-Work Integration
  • Evaluation of Advanced Testing Technologies
  • Algorithmic Decision-Making in HR
  • Human-Automation Teaming
  • AI and Work
  • Economic and Employment Transitions
  • Sustainable Work and Environmental Psychology

Timeline

  • October 1, 2026: Submission window opens
  • October 31, 2026: Submission deadline (8:00 p.m. U.S. Eastern Time)

item.title: The Generative Workplace: The Lived Experience of Generative AI at Work
item.content:encoded:
Louis Tay, Purdue University

Sarah Bankins, Macquarie University

Markus Langer, University of Freiburg

This special issue examines how generative AI is reshaping the subjective experience of work across individuals, teams, and organizations. Rather than focusing on technical capabilities, it centers on what it feels like to work with AI systems like ChatGPT and Claude—how these tools influence engagement, relationships, identity, and organizational norms as adoption rapidly increases among knowledge workers worldwide.

The issue seeks empirically rigorous, theory-grounded research that closely observes generative AI in actual workplace settings. Priority is given to field research within organizations, implementation studies tracking deployment experiences, longitudinal designs, and rigorous qualitative research. Vignette studies, cross-sectional surveys of convenience samples, and conceptual papers without data are out of scope.

Submissions should articulate theoretical mechanisms for how generative AI changes work experiences, provide evidence credible for practitioners, and explicitly discuss practical impact for employees, managers, HR leaders, and policymakers.

Appel publié par Personnel Psychology. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Experience of work: Cognitive offloading and changes in effort, flow, and engagement; experiences of autonomy, competence, and ownership over AI-generated or AI-assisted output; changes to the meaning of work; skill development versus skill atrophy; work intensification versus work-life balance; changing nature of expertise; calibration of trust and over- or under-reliance; professional identity as roles shift
  • Workplace relationships: Generative AI as a team member and its impact on social and working dynamics; emerging disclosure norms; trust, attribution, and competence judgments when AI is involved; migration of help-seeking and sensemaking from colleagues to AI tools; effects on collaboration, collegiality, reciprocity, informal mentorship, and organizational cohesion
  • Training and development: Use and experience of AI as a trainer, coach, and mentor; development and declines in knowledge, skills, and abilities with AI use; lasting effects of AI-based training; comparisons of human trainers versus AI trainers; design of AI-based training and transfer to job performance
  • Leadership: Leaders' use of generative AI for communication and the authenticity dilemma of machine-mediated empathy, vision, and feedback; leader decision processes with AI input; generative AI systems operating autonomously or in hybrid arrangements; what it feels like to be managed by generative AI
  • Organizational culture: Emergent norms of acceptable generative AI use; psychological safety around disclosing versus concealing use; experience of monitoring and surveillance of workers' AI use or non-use; equity and felt divide between users and non-users; implications for inclusive workplaces

Timeline

  • August 1, 2027: Submission window opens
  • August 27, 2027: Submission deadline
  • August 31, 2027: Submission window closes
